Salvation Army opens thrift store in St. Clair Shores
articles.content: Business was brisk at the new St. Clair Shores Salvation Army Thrift Store for its grand opening Nov. 6. Located at 24301 Harper Avenue, just north of Little Mack Avenue, the new 10,000 square foot store has a boutique vibe and offers plenty of great deals on clothing, housewares and more. Community members gathered in front of the new store for a ribbon cutting ceremony Friday morning and customers were ready to get inside and browse as soon as the doors opened. “The Salvation Army has a longstanding connection to the St. Clair Shores community, and this new location allows us to continue serving local shoppers in a refreshed retail space,” said Envoy Jacqulynn Idzior, administrator for The Salvation Army Southeast Michigan Adult Rehabilitation Center. “The new boutique-style store will offer a thoughtfully curated selection of secondhand merchandise for a more elevated thrift shopping experience.” The thrift store, which relocated from a spot further north at 31015 Harper Avenue, will be stocked with untouched and curated merchandise, including new and gently used clothing, shoes, handbags, quality housewares, furniture, collectibles and more. The original store will remain open through Nov. 25 and leading up to its closure, merchandise will be incrementally marked down until the sales floor is cleared. The St. Clair Shores Salvation Army Thrift Store will be open from 9 a.m. to 9 p.m. and donations will be accepted from 10 a.m. to 7 p.m. Monday through Saturday. Proceeds from all 30 Salvation Army thrift stores fund the ARC, located at 1627 W. Fort Street in Detroit. The ARC provides substance-abuse rehabilitation, nutritious meals, leisure activities, individual counseling and spiritual direction, along with resources to develop life skills.

After the US midterm rout of Trumpism, the world struggles to trust America again
articles.description: After the US midterm rout of Trumpism, the world struggles to trust America again AP News What will a lame-duck Donald Trump get up to overseas? The Economist From Iran to trade: how the US midterms impact the rest of the world Reuters U.S. Foes React to the GOP’s Midterm Wipeout Foreign Policy In These Midterms, Foreign Policy Mattered Council on Foreign Relations
articles.content: LONDON (AP) — For Joe Reeve, the midterm afterglow faded fast. The London startup founder was among the wave around the Trump-weary world awakening to the stunning news that Americans had sharply rejected President Donald Trump’s fist-in-the-eye stewardship of the United States that had started a war with Iran, forged no peace in Ukraine or the Mideast and made gas and food so expensive. Voters, Reeve saw online, had flipped control of both houses of Congress, handing the power to check the president to his rival Democrats. American democracy, 250 years on, had survived the Trump era. But a deep and profound distrust of the United States had survived the vote, too. And from national leaders to aspiring American immigrants, no one seemed confident that change was afoot. “What everybody’s learned,” Reeve, 29, the husband of a Ukrainian, said a day later in an interview, “is that America’s system does allow for these wild swings. We all know, now, that America has an ability to rotate on a dime and spit in our faces.” Interviews by The Associated Press around the world since the vote revealed a sense that “one election alone does not restore anything,” as Kim So-jung, 49, an office worker in Yongin, South Korea, put it. “We have to see what they actually do, and see that they are doing something different to gain at least a little trust back.” That 77 million Americans voted to elect Trump to a second term, along with the administration’s combative conduct on his tariff war, Israel’s conduct in Gaza, immigration and Iran, had already shaken trust in America around the world. By the time Americans awakened Wednesday, global leaders and regular people from Europe to Australia had moved beyond the “wow” to a reckoning with the reality that Trump still retains enormous powers. “Quite frankly, Trump has largely governed without Congress for the past two years. Why should that change now?” German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said a few hours after voters flipped control of the House and Senate. Trump’s apparent detachment from the results and his focus on building projects in the days before and after the drubbing did little to calm speculation about how he governs. He could dissociate completely, some observers said. Or he could lean into foreign policy and become even less predictable. “For the country’s allies, the question isn’t whether America is back,” Ian Bremmer, president and founder of Eurasia Group, wrote in Think China. “It’s back to what — and for how long?” The stunning midterm elections were not enough to reverse policies that have strained economies and finances and put dreams of making it in America on hold for many across the globe. Trump’s tariff war has roiled markets and economies. He canceled humanitarian aid for millions and upended the world’s postwar order. Under Trump, American immigration policy turned violent and deadly — and makes the U.S. look to many like a place better avoided. There was no sign of Trump letting up. On Friday, he promoted longtime aide Stephen Miller, a key architect of his hard-line immigration policy, to replace Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff. “I don’t think all is forgiven,” ReadtheLine.ca Editor Jen Gerson said during an online discussion Thursday. “The President’s hold on power over two terms is — and ought to remain — a warning sign to Canada and to all of America’s allies.” America’s political and economic uncertainty can affect businesses like Synetica, an Indonesian tech company, one of its business development managers said. “For me, regaining trust means seeing America consistently respect democratic institutions, the rule of law and its international partners,” Aditya Surya, 40, of Yogyakarta, Indonesia, told the AP. “The election is a good start, but what happens next matters a lot more.” Many eyes are trained on whether the Democrats can reverse Trump’s costly tariff regime as the incoming majority has promised in its 100 days agenda — and whether Trump accepts or vetoes any such changes. Hamish McIntyre, an Australian beef producer, suspects not. With a Southern Hemisphere spring harvest underway in parts of Australia, farmers are grappling with diesel prices inflated by the Iran war, contributing to what the government forecasts will be a 39% drop in large farm profits. “The midterm result is unlikely, in itself, to fundamentally change the direction of U.S. tariff policy,” said McIntyre, president of the National Farmers’ Federation agricultural advocacy group. The election, he added, does not “prevent the administration from continuing to pursue its broader trade agenda.” Ivan Slatkine, president of the Federation of Romandie Enterprises in French-speaking Switzerland, said he’s heartened that the election showed America’s institutions remain robust. That’s worth some confidence, he added. “Let us not be naive,” Slatkine said. “The ‘America First’ concept is not going to be abandoned anytime soon, and I doubt the new majority will reverse all the decisions made by the president.” Hong Kong businessman Danny Lau gained some hope from the elections. More than 30% of the orders received by his aluminum-coating factory in the southern Chinese city of Dongguan come from American clients. But his business was paying a tariff of nearly 81%. “Trump started the tariff war,” Lau said. “If he loses his influence, would that help at all on the tariff front? At the very least, hopefully he won’t raise them any further.” Michael Lu, CEO of gift-box producer Brothersbox in southern China, said he believed political tensions remain elevated, particularly after Washington’s earlier trade war against China. But no matter who won the midterms, he didn’t expect drastic changes in Washington’s overall stance against China. The U.S. accounts for roughly 20% of Lu’s company’s business. The political shift in the U.S. doesn’t change the fact that “continuing to strengthen the alliance and economic relations with the U.S. is essential for Japan,” said Yoshinobu Tsutsui, chairman of Keidanren, the Japan Business Federation, a lobby group that represents 1,500 companies. He said he expects Trump to come out even stronger, not weaker, with the Democrats in control of Congress. Ambika, an Indian citizen who asked to be identified only by her last name, works in IT in America and has long yearned to make America her permanent home. But Trump’s immigration crackdown and latest green card restrictions have given her pause. “Recent visa policy changes have left me worried,” she said this week while visiting family in India. “I don’t know if ... the midterm results would lead to any policy change that could benefit those of us who want to move to the U.S.” There’s no more accurate look at how America is changing than U.S. elections. And these midterms produced the biggest shift in political power since the post-Watergate election of 1974. “Time and again, we are presented with these chances for change, only for greed to snatch defeat from the jaws of victory,” U.K.-based commentator Martin McSweeney wrote on his “Truth Matters” Substack at 5 a.m. the day after the election. “Will this time be different? That’s up to the American people, and that makes me very nervous given past experience.” This story has been corrected to reflect that the name of Ian Bremmer’s organization is Eurasia Group, not Eurasian Group. Associated Press writers across the globe contributed to this report. They include: Kanis Leung and Thomas Chan in Hong Kong, Rod McGuirk in Melbourne, Sheikh Saaliq in New Delhi, Kim Tong-hyung in Seoul, South Korea, Yuri Kageyama in Tokyo, Edna Tarigan in Jakarta, and Jamey Keaten in Geneva.

articles.title: Democrats will hold most legislative trifectas since 1984
articles.description: Along with a dramatic change in congressional majorities on Election Day, an analysis from the National Conference of State Legislatures showed large shifts in legislative majorities around the country, flipping from a majority of Republican legislatures to majority Democratic. Democrats also now hold a large number of trifectas, said the conference’s Katy Owens Hubler, meaning […]
articles.content: State Rep. Ranjeev Puri (D-Canton) steps to the podium in Detroit with Senate Majority Leader Winnie Brinks (D-Grand Rapids) after Democrats retook the majority on the Michigan House and retained control of the Senate. Puri is on track to be the next Speaker of the House, while Brinks was elected at lieutenant governor earlier Wednesday, Nov. 4, 2026. (Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan Advance)Along with a dramatic change in congressional majorities on Election Day, an analysis from the National Conference of State Legislatures showed large shifts in legislative majorities around the country, flipping from a majority of Republican legislatures to majority Democratic. Democrats also now hold a large number of trifectas, said the conference’s Katy Owens Hubler, meaning they control both chambers of the state legislature alongside a Democratic governor. Heading into the elections, Republicans held 23 trifectas nationwide, and that was cut down to 17. Democrats now will have 22 trifectas beginning in January. “This is a high point for Democratic trifectas going back to before 1984,” said Owens Hubler, director of the elections and redistricting program at the organization. NCSL, the nonpartisan organization that represents and supports state legislatures nationwide, held a press event on Friday to discuss the election results. Prior to the election, Republicans controlled 28 state legislative chambers while Democrats controlled 18. Now, Democrats will control 24 chambers and Republicans will have 21. It’s the largest shift for Democrats since 2010, according to NCSL. Votes are still being counted in some races, and results remain unofficial until certified in the coming weeks. The legislative chambers that flipped or are expected to flip from Republican to Democrat include Houses in Alaska, Georgia, Michigan, Minnesota, North Carolina and Texas, and the Senate in Pennsylvania. Both chambers flipped in Arizona, New Hampshire and Wisconsin. That leaves Alaska, Georgia, North Carolina and Texas as divided chambers that were previously both controlled by Republicans, although some races in Alaska and North Carolina remain too close to call. “Going back to 2012, we have had both legislative chambers in all of the Southern states be red,” said Owens Hubler. “This new map … is pretty new and pretty different from the trend that we had been seeing for the last dozen years.” At least five governor seats already officially turned from Republican to Democrat — Georgia, Iowa, Ohio, Nevada and Texas. Alaska is expected to elect a Democratic governor as well once all of the ballots are tabulated, the NCSL team said. “If that is the case, we’re looking at 30 Democratic governors and 20 Republican governors,” Owens Hubler said. “Again, they haven’t had the majority of governors’ mansions since before 2010, and 30 is quite a large number for them.” Stateline reporter Kelcie Moseley-Morris can be reached at kmoseley@stateline.org. This story was originally produced by Stateline, which is part of States Newsroom, a nonprofit news network which includes Michigan Advance, and is supported by grants and a coalition of donors as a 501c(3) public charity.

articles.content: Binance’s chief financial officer Kaiser Ng is leaving the cryptocurrency exchange. According to Bloomberg, co-CEO Yi He said in a statement that Ng’s departure will allow him to “pursue a new venture after more than five years at Binance,” and that a transition plan has been “implemented over the last half year.” The announcement comes barely more than a week after hackers stole $6.3 billion worth of cryptocurrency from Binance users. The company froze withdrawals for several days; after accounts were unfrozen, users withdrew a net $3.6 billion in the first few hours. Binance and the FBI blamed a North Korean group called TraderTraitor for the hack. The company also said that it would cover all losses, promising, “Binance will bear the financial impact of the stolen funds. These losses will not be passed on to users.” Ng will be replaced as CFO by Justin Yek. articles.title: Hines ready to reel in costs, check Trump
articles.content: Christina Hines doesn’t have time to bask in her election victory Tuesday to take the 10th District congressional seat in Macomb and Oakland counties. The Democratic congresswoman-elect is preparing to take office in January and has set up a meeting with former congresswoman Candice Miller, reached out to Republican U.S. Rep. Lisa McClain and was scheduled to travel to Washington D.C. on Sunday for 10 days of orientation. Hines, 36, of Warren, flipped the seat to Democratic by defeating Republican Michael Bouchard, 32, of Rochester Hills, and contributed to Democrats gaining control of the U.S. House of Representatives to serve as a check on Republican President Donald Trump, whom she has been allowed to “reign like a king.” The seat is currently held by GOP U.S. Rep. John James, who lost the race for govenor. She said she wants to hit the ground running working to reduce costs for constituents after she takes the oath office Jan. 3. That will require reining in Trump because the Constitution allows it, she said. “We can’t keep letting the executive reign like a king,” Hines said. “We have to be the checks and balances that the Constitution calls for. Congress needs to take back the power of the purse. That is very clearly articulated in our Constitution.” Congress has failed to wield the power it has to rein in Trump on the Iran war, she said. “Right now, we need to stand up to the president,” she said. “He made a promise to the American people to not start these endless wars. We need to be the force that comes in and changes that direction and that course.” But Hines said she harbors concerns that the next two years will resemble theatrics over substance. “I’m really worried that people are going to get people locked into the political theater,” she said. “I do believe in accountability and I do want to make sure that some things that happened under this administration can never happen again, like the weaponization of the Justice Department. I don’t care what party the president is from, that should never happen,” she said. She reiterated what will be her top focus. “I’ll be talking a lot about how we need to end this war with Iran and about how we have to end the trade war with Canada, end the tariffs,” Hines said. “Those things are costing families here more money, whether it’s the gas (prices) and higher diesel prices raising prices at the stores, or whether it’s tariffs costing us to lose jobs and raise the price of goods.” Southeast Michigan has been dramatically impacted by Trump’s trade policies, she said. “We really do need to take a look at how we can use tariffs or trade policy in general to protect workers here, to keep jobs here, but also to lift up standards all over the world because if you keep letting jobs go overseas it becomes a race to a bottom, with these other countries that don’t have to protect their workers or pay them a living wage,” she said. Another priority is to “fight the corruption” caused by “corporations buying off all of our politicians, that raises our costs, too.” She also wants to focus early on reducing health care costs, including reversing the cuts in tax credits for those under the Affordable Care Act that have resulted in higher premiums for millions across the nation, and protecting Medicare and Medicaid. She said caps can be put on out of pocket costs and premium costs, and better prescription drug prices should be negotiated. “I will work with anybody to make it (health care) more affordable and acceptable for every single American,” she said. Medicaid cuts passed by Republicans will soon be showing their negative impacts. “We’re also going to see rural health systems all over this country close because Medicaid is propping health systems …, especially in rural America, and a lot of those places are represented by Republicans,” Hines said. “Over the next year, I think we’re going to have to see a lot of people from both sides of the aisle coming to the table and figuring out a real, bipartisan solution to this, and I know I’m only a freshman, but I’m hope that I can be one the leaders and the voices at the table to fix it for the people of our district.” Also important to Hines, who was a prosecutor for 10 years in Washtenaw County, is improving “background checks and closing those loopholes” for gun owners in the battle to fight crime. “I’ve seen the impact of gun violence first hand,” she said. “I want responsible gun owners to be able to have their guns, and they can have as many guns as they want. But we got to make sure that people who are criminals or with mental health issues cannot get their hands on a gun.” Regarding McClain, who is a conservative Republican and strong advocate of Trump, Hines said she hopes she can work with her on issues such as protecting Selfridge Air National Guard Base in Harrison Township and Lake St. Clair. Macomb County Executive Mark Hackel praised Hines, saying she will be more interested in progress, not politics. “She’s going to be an incredible asset for Macomb County,” Hackel said. “She understands it, she gets it. “She’s in a kind of a swing district, so she’s not going to be pushing a political agenda. I think it’s going to be more focused on Macomb County economic development,” such as the defense industry including aerospace. In defeating Bouchard, the son of Oakland County Sheriff Mike Bouchard, Hines collected 60.2% of the vote in Macomb County and 51.7% of the tally in Oakland County. Macomb comprises about 89% of the district. “I think people really wanted someone that was focused on costs and fighting for this community,” Hines said of her victory. “That’s what we focused on. We didn’t get lost in the bickering and politics. We really tried to keep our message about lowering costs for people, and I think that resonated and I think people felt I was the one that they could trust.” Hines, who is married with three children, during the campaign touted her vow to “protect families” by delivering critical funding for law enforcement to prevent violent crime and keep our seniors and kids safe online.” She also said it was important that Hines, virtually a lifelong resident of the county, has many friends and family members in the district. “This campaign started with a simple truth: that working families in our district are sick of being left behind by corrupt politicians in Washington and deserve someone who will actually put their needs first,” Hines said in a statement following her win. “Over the last 18 months, I have been moved by the thousands of people who have told me their stories, shared their struggles, and demanded more from their leaders. Your words have stayed with me throughout this entire campaign and I will carry them with me to Washington.” In his statement following the election, Bouchard said, “I got into this race because I love this country. America is the greatest country that has ever existed and election results going to the other party, do not diminish America’s shine. I will endeavor to ensure we remain that beacon on the hill throughout the world. Our promise is not political, it is in you. It is in freedom and our democracy.” The district’s boundaries include Macomb County south of Hall Road, Shelby Township, Utica, a part of Macomb Township, and Rochester and Rochester Hills.

articles.title: Airstrikes kill more than 2 dozen people near Yemen’s capital, Houthis say
articles.description: Airstrikes kill more than 2 dozen people near Yemen’s capital, Houthis say AP News Houthis say at least 33 killed in Saudi air strike BBC More Than 50 Killed in Yemen in One of the Deadliest 24 Hours of the War The New York Times Yemeni gov’t forces report advances as Houthis say deadly strikes hit Sanaa Al Jazeera An airstrike has killed 22 people near Yemen's capital, Houthi official says ABC News - Breaking News,
articles.content: CAIRO (AP) — Airstrikes hit homes in a village near Yemen’s capital, Sanaa, on Saturday, killing at least 27 people and wounding 36 others, mostly women and children, a spokesman for Yemen’s Houthi-run Health Ministry said. Speaking to The Associated Press, Anees al-Asbahi said the death toll is expected to rise as search and rescue efforts continue and accused Saudi Arabia of carrying out the strikes on al-Shariya. Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree, the Houthi military spokesperson, claimed in a statement later Saturday that the group had carried out attacks against Saudi Arabia in response to the strikes on the village as well as another deadly attack Friday on a market in southwestern Yemen. The AP could not independently verify the Houthis’ claims, and Saudi Arabia’s Information Ministry did not immediately reply to AP requests for comment. Saturday’s toll reflected the rapid worsening of Yemen’s civil war, where a yearslong truce fell apart over the summer. Fighting has escalated between the Iranian-backed Houthis — who control Sanaa, the north and the west of the country — and their Saudi-backed opponents based in the south and east. On Friday, an airstrike in a market in southern Yemen killed at least 30 people, according to Houthi officials. The Houthis and Yemen’s Saudi-backed military each blamed the other for that strike. Footage from Houthi-run Al-Masirah TV showed hospital staff carrying limp bodies of multiple young children from ambulances after Saturday’s strikes. One little girl’s head had been cleaved open. Other children lay on stretchers, bloodied and bandaged as staff tended to them. Footage from the farming village — located in Houthi-ruled territory about 15 kilometers (10 miles) northeast of Sanaa — showed the rubble of destroyed houses and dust filling the air as people hid in nearby agricultural fields. Al-Asbahi told Al-Masirah that civilians were still buried under the rubble of houses, and that subsequent strikes targeted emergency workers as they tried to pull survivors out of the wreckage. Footage showed one wounded man covered in dust and wearing a first responder’s orange vest being helped out of an ambulance. The renewed fighting has raised fears that Yemen will be dragged back into the horrors of a civil war that has lasted for more than a decade and created one of the world’s worst humanitarian disasters. The war began when the Houthis stormed out of the north in 2014 and seized the capital, driving out the internationally recognized government. Saudi Arabia assembled a coalition backing the government, waging a yearslong campaign of air bombardment that brought it international condemnation over civilian deaths. The conflict has killed at least 150,000 people, according to the U.N., along with widespread deaths from hunger and disease outbreaks. The lines of control in the country changed little for years, and a truce was reached in 2022. The relative quiet, however, collapsed over the summer when the Houthis launched new offensives in response, they said, to Saudi Arabia’s continued blockade of their territory. The rebels made a lightning advance capturing much of Yemen’s Red Sea coast and strategic islands in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. At the same time, they have stepped up strikes on Saudi Arabia, targeting oil and military infrastructure and shipping in the Red Sea. Meanwhile, the Saudi-led coalition has said it has been carrying out airstrikes in Houthi-held territory, targeting the rebels’ military infrastructure. The heaviest ground fighting has centered around Taiz, a strategic, government-held southern city that the Houthis have now encircled, worsening an already dire humanitarian situation among civilians. Residents are struggling to secure drinking water and food supplies as the Houthis restrict movement into the city.

articles.content: Concerns are being raised that neither the Commerce Department nor Nvidia are doing their due diligence when it comes to vetting Chinese firms cleared to handle the company’s H200 AI chips. According to The New York Times, New Matrix is on the list of approved firms, yet its offices are empty, “a hollow gray shell with wires dangling from the ceiling where lights should be.” In fact, the paper could find little evidence that the company exists in any meaningful way: > Only scant information can be found online about New Matrix, which was created 17 months ago. At the building that New Matrix lists as its address, a company directory does not include the firm. At the nearby property management agency for the industrial park, a receptionist and a manager both said they had no record of the company. What little information can be found about New Matrix is concerning. Its owners have ties to a Chinese private equity firm that has been blacklisted by the US government since 2024. And according to the Times, this is not a rare lapse in oversight, but a troubling pattern of companies connected to entities with national-security-related trade restrictions being approved to purchase Nvidia chips. Nvidia had been restricted from selling chips to China during the Biden presidency. But the Trump administration relaxed those limits after Nvidia agreed to give the government a 15-percent cut of all sales. The company’s CEO, Jensen Huang, also launched an intense lobbying campaign and was apparently targeted by China’s Ministry of State Security in a spying plot.

According to The New York Times, New Matrix is on the list of approved firms, yet its offices are empty, “a hollow gray shell with wires dangling from the ceiling where lights should be.” In fact, the paper could find little evidence that the company exists in any meaningful way: > Only scant information can be found online about New Matrix, which was created 17 months ago. At the building that New Matrix lists as its address, a company directory does not include the firm. At the nearby property management agency for the industrial park, a receptionist and a manager both said they had no record of the company. What little information can be found about New Matrix is concerning. Its owners have ties to a Chinese private equity firm that has been blacklisted by the US government since 2024. And according to the Times, this is not a rare lapse in oversight, but a troubling pattern of companies connected to entities with national-security-related trade restrictions being approved to purchase Nvidia chips. Nvidia had been restricted from selling chips to China during the Biden presidency. But the Trump administration relaxed those limits after Nvidia agreed to give the government a 15-percent cut of all sales. The company’s CEO, Jensen Huang, also launched an intense lobbying campaign and was apparently targeted by China’s Ministry of State Security in a spying plot.

articles.content: Today, I’m talking with Alex Stamos, chief security officer at Cognition and longtime cybersecurity expert, about what a mess cybersecurity is right now. This episode is part one of a special series looking at AI in real life. I’ve always enjoyed talking to Alex because he’s so direct, and you’re going to hear him say that the multibillion-dollar cybersecurity industry as we’ve known it is essentially overdue to the unrelenting, AI-boosted waves of hacks, breaches, and attacks — and this is only the beginning of how much AI is changing security. --- [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/chorus/uploads/chorus_asset/file/24792604/The_Verge_Decoder_Tileart.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here. Not a subscriber? You can sign up here. --- Both private actors and also state actors, like Russia or North Korea, are breaking into systems all over thanks to AI helping them both detect and exploit vulnerabilities all at the same time. It’s got a real frontier feel to it, Alex notes, just like the ’90s, when the whole idea of an always-online world was brand-new. That much disruption means a lot of places where bad guys can get in while everyone else is left scrambling. Alex isn’t a doomer in the long run, but he does think we’re in for a “dark age” while we try to figure out how on earth to adapt to the new era. There’s a lot going on here — we even got all the way to how AI-powered misinformation and slop might be managed on our social networks. Before we get going, do me a favor and subscribe to Decoder on YouTube, where we put out new episodes every Monday and Thursday. Okay: Alex Stamos on how AI is upending cybersecurity. Here we go. This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity. Alex Stamos, you’re the chief security officer at Cognition. You’re also a lecturer at Stanford University Cyber Policy Center. Welcome back to Decoder. Hey, thanks for having me, man. I’m excited to talk to you. It’s been a long time since you and I chatted in what you might call the “content moderation era” of internet policy discourse. I feel like you and I talked a lot about how all that was working, about election security, all those sorts of things. We’re in a new era of big problems on the internet, particularly around cyber defense, cybersecurity. You’ve been thinking about this stuff a lot. You referred to the past few weeks as “security awareness month.” Tell me what’s going on. Just give me the lay of land right now. October is traditionally security awareness month. Lots of companies run events and deal both internally and then tell people, “Change your password, use multiple passwords, use a password manager.” What has happened over the last month is we’ve had a couple of these big bugs, PHP, Node and such. What’s been less discussed is a huge number of companies have been breached. You have a series of AI-related companies, the neoclouds that have been breached in succession. You have the Binance hack, which is the largest heist of anything in human history. You have the Cursor incident where one of the things that’s going on here is these hacks are being chained together. From what we know right now, one of the companies that was broken into was Fireworks, which is a prominent provider of AI services to a number of companies. From the Fireworks hack, API keys were stolen that allowed people to break into Cursor. Once they got into Cursor, they then pushed a bad plugin, which went to 5,000 more companies and that caused 5,000 potential breaches. It’s just this kind of permanent continuous breach that is going on throughout the tech industry. A CISO friend of mine said to a bunch of us, “Is anybody else tired?” And everybody said yes, because effectively we have been at DEFCON 2 for all of October and now going into November. I’m going to ask you some really dumb questions here. Who is behind all these attacks? Is it Russia? Is it North Korea? Do we know? It’s a variety of different groups. It is not just because adversaries have decided, but what has happened is, from my perspective, we are at the start of the takeoff of adversary capability enabled by AI, that the open-weight models have now gotten to the point at which you can automate most of the kill chain. This “kill chain” term is something we stole from the military. In the military, they mean to actually kill something. They’re the steps you do to blow something up. In cyber, the kill chain is the things you do to have an effect on a target. So to steal information, to turn something off, to steal money, to steal Bitcoin. Traditionally, you do research upfront, you look at a piece of software, you find a vulnerability, you write exploits, and you do that all way ahead of time. And then you have a human being go and take that stuff you built and deploy it against either one target — because maybe you’re a government and you’re going against Lockheed Martin or you’re going against another government or you’re a ransomware actor — and you take all that work you did and you deploy it against hundreds or thousands of targets really fast. Now with AI, what’s happening is this kill chain has inverted where you can run an AI system that just goes hog wild and it looks at the targets and it finds the bugs in real time and it writes the exploits in real time and it breaks into these companies. One of the things that’s happening is that these systems are going and they’re so good at finding bugs that they are finding the bugs in real time and writing the exploits in real time. The system that everybody’s talking about is not the only one, but the system we’re talking about is a thing called ARTEX, which is a Chinese open-source tool that anybody can go look at. There’s an English translation on GitHub that you can check out. And if you power it on the back end by something like an obliterated GLM-5.3, it will let you break into a shocking number of organizations. This started with three South Korean banks. This week, about 200 more companies have been hit. I’ve been helping a couple of companies. Cognition is not an incident response company, but we do go in and help people fix their bugs afterwards by using our tools. It is shocking the companies that are getting hit by something you could just download. It has been a long time since you’ve been able to go and just download an open-source tool and break into multi-billion dollar companies. It’s like the ‘90s. That’s- That’s what I was thinking about. I think about Windows in the late ‘90s, early 2000s when it was a security disaster. I started saying this actually in the beginning of this year, that it’s an incredibly exciting and terrifying time, because the last time it felt like this was when I was a much younger man and I would go to the very early DEFCONs. DEFCON these days is like 40,000–60,000 people. Back then [in the 1990s] it was a couple hundred people and it was one track and you’d go in and somebody would give a talk and you’d leave the room and you’d think, “Every company in the world is vulnerable to this attack.” The difference was that the entire world didn’t run on the internet. You could go do bad things, but you couldn’t ruin the world and you certainly couldn’t automate it in the way you can now. It’s back to those days where tools you could just get and build yourself could do crazy things. It’s back to the Wild West days. Back in those days, there were a couple hundred people who had those skills and we were all in one room in Las Vegas and most of them were actually good guys. They didn’t want to be criminals. And now you have a much larger ecosystem of people, many of whom live in places where the law enforcement can’t touch and who have a big economic incentive and have access to these tools. The other big thing is they no longer have to use frontier models that have protections, that have logs that are available to law enforcement. My M5 Mac Ultra Studio finally showed up and I’ve been running a quantized obliterated GLM-5.3 and oh my God, what you can do is incredible. You mentioned the economics of frontier models. The economy of cyber is one of those things that has gotten sophisticated over the years. One of the things that our systems got safer is you could pay the number of people at DEF CON a whole bunch of money to protect all the systems and it was economically smart to pay them to be defenders instead of attackers. I’m just rewinding my own brain through this history. There was a long conversation in our industry about security through obscurity by hiding all the bugs and hiding all the code versus open source and being really transparent. There was an etiquette that developed about how to reveal the bugs and when to give people notification. There were transparency reports and bug bounties. You could call it an etiquette, you could call it an economy. We built a culture around cybersecurity and cyber defense and how the attackers and defenders would operate. What you are describing changes it all for a whole number of reasons, but the one that sticks out to me is the economics of it. I can go buy a Mac Studio, I can get an open-weight model and I can just start and that does not place me inside of the culture. There’s not going to be some old man, an Obi-Wan Kenobi saying, “Here’s how you act like a cybersecurity Jedi.” I’m just going to start doing stuff. Tell me how that’s changing right now. Effectively, the last era of security from my perspective started with the Microsoft, the Bill Gates “trustworthy computing” memo in the early 2000s. And that is when we started designing how we do software security and these big companies, Microsoft and Oracle and then later Amazon and Salesforce and these folks, started hiring ex-hackers. I was part of that generation of the ex-hackers who were at DEF CON and Black Hat and got hired by the companies to go break their stuff. We started coming up with responsible disclosure, bug bounties, consulting companies, so the Foundstone and @stake and then Mandiant and CrowdStrike, these companies grow up and we get this huge industry that is now RSA and Black Hat. This multi-billion dollar security industry grew up in the 2000s and 2010s. That era is over, like you said, because it was based upon a couple of assumptions. One was that there was a hierarchy of skillsets of people who could do this stuff. You had the script kiddies who could download tools to do things and then the next level up of the people who could write those tools and that was a more rarefied skill set. There were the vulnerability researchers and then there were the gods, and that god tier was in the hundreds of people and those are the people who could do the really, really good vulnerability research, who could write the really, really good shell code, who could reverse engineer patches from Microsoft or somebody like that. There was also the assumption that there were a limited number of people who could be operational in an attack. If you wanted to build an attack team, then you have a small R&D component and then you have a much larger operational component. If you were a professional attack team at U.S. Cyber Command, at Russia SVR, at Chinese MSS, that you build the structure of your R&D team of elite people and then your less elite operational people, and that was copied then by the Russian ransomware actors. You have to have a conspiracy of people to do this stuff. A lot of this stuff also fell apart with the invention of Bitcoin because one of the assumptions was that you had to have people who could launder money and Bitcoin meant that nerds could launder money. So that started to change the economics of the entire thing. articles.description: Dearborn Mayor Abdullah Hammoud says the city saw record-breaking midterm voter turnout during the recent midterm elections. He says it was in an effort to elect Abdul El-Sayed as the first Muslim U.S. Senator despite the heavy anti-Arab and anti-Muslim rhetoric surrounding his campaign.
articles.content: Dearborn Mayor Abdullah Hammoud addresses members of the press in November, 2026(Etai Smotrich-Barr / Michigan Public)Dearborn Mayor Abdullah Hammoud says the city experienced the highest voter turnout in its history during the recent midterm elections."When we got notice that we were running out of registration forms at certain precincts, that in fact, some precincts ran out of ballots, I was like, 'what is happening?'" Hammoud recalled.Speaking with NPR’s Morning Edition host Leila Fadel, Hammoud attributed the historic surge at the polls to the election of Abdul El-Sayed, a Michigan Democrat who recently made history as the first Muslim U.S. Senator.However, the mayor emphasized that it was not just El-Sayed’s identity that mobilized Dearborn's majority-Arab and significant Muslim community, but his policies."I think what got them to the polls are candidates who centered the issues of working class families, like many of the American and Muslim American families right here in the city of Dearborn," he said.El-Sayed campaigned heavily on fighting political corruption and prioritizing domestic community investments over foreign military spending.The election cycle contained significant anti-Arab and anti-Muslim vitriol from high-profile political figures, which Hammoud noted caused real fear among some of the city's youth and vulnerable residents. Despite this, he says El-Sayed’s victory proves that voters rejected bigoted rhetoric."I think it means that Michiganders believe in America that's big enough for all of us," Hammoud said. "What doesn't matter is the direction… you pray. What matters more is the direction in which you wish to lead".He also highlighted El-Sayed's own messaging on the campaign trail. "I think Dr. Abdul said it best," Hammoud said. "He said, 'My faith and my ethnicity is not why gas prices are all time high. My faith and my ethnicity is not why the grocery bill keeps climbing, not why utility costs are skyrocketing.' I think we have an America that is big enough to see through the smoke screen of the bigotry and be welcoming of all people."Hammoud views the midterm election results as a rejection of the divisive politics of the past decade."And I wholeheartedly believe that the election results this week are a response to the Trump presidency of 2016. It took us ten years to build this moment, but I think it's finally arrived, and we have an opportunity to do something beautiful across America".

articles.title: What's the history behind the MSU v. U-M rivalry?
articles.description: The in-state rivalry between Michigan's two biggest schools started before football was a sport.
articles.content: FILE - Michigan State quarterback Aidan Chiles, left, prepares to throw as Michigan linebacker Jaishawn Barham chases him in the second half of an NCAA college football game, Saturday, Oct. 26, 2024, in Ann Arbor, Mich.(Jose Juarez / AP)Emma from Port Huron asked us:"Like all Michiganders, I grew up with the MSU versus U of M rivalry. As a proud Spartan graduate, I remember many iconic moments like trouble with the snap and Kenneth Walker's five touchdown game. My question is, what are the origins of this rivalry? Were there moments early on that escalated the tension between the two universities?"In the modern era, friends and family throughout the state gather together in the fall for an annual tradition. It goes something like this.One calls the other, "Little Brother."The other responds, "Walmart Wolverines."And then, "Michigan vs. Everybody." Followed by, "Okay, Connor Stalions." The phantom second. A missed two-point conversion. Braylon Edwards triple overtime. Trouble with the snap. The tunnel brawl.This is the shorthand and shared language spoken by all U-M and MSU fans throughout the state.It's personal because it's family. But why and how did this rivalry begin? For the answer we turned to Chris Vannini. He's a reporter for The Athletic who wrote about the origins of the interschool strife, and the series of events that deepened the rivalry. Here's what he told us:The rivalry began with the founding of Michigan State"The second Constitution for the State of Michigan in 1850 established the creation of an agricultural school, and there was some argument over where that school should go. The University of Michigan wanted to have it, the State Agricultural Society potentially wanted to put it somewhere else. They eventually decide they'll put it within ten miles of Lansing, which is the remote capital at that point in time. And ultimately in 1855, the Agricultural College of the State of Michigan was created, and would become later Michigan State University."And even in the ensuing years and a couple of decades, the University of Michigan attempted to kind of acquire the school or shut down part of the school or grab parts of it. And so these conflicts continued in the many decades in the late 1800s, after the school had been founded."The football rivalry began in the early 20th century, before MSU was in the Big Ten, but just as their program was getting good"Michigan was upset that it perceived Michigan State to be violating various rules, whether that involved payments to players, whether that involved academics, stuff that we talk about now, a hundred years later, these arguments have been made. And so as Michigan State started to get better, Michigan didn't want a lot of schools in the Big Ten to play Michigan State. They didn't want to validate the program, help the program grow and get more attention for these various reasons that it felt like it wasn't following Big Ten rules, even though it wasn't a member of the conference. And by the 1930s, schools outside of Michigan in the Western Conference basically refused to play Michigan State as a result, in part because Michigan State was so good and in part because of the rule breaking. And Michigan State long suspected there was a Michigan led boycott of the games. "But Michigan would keep playing Michigan State, for a couple of reasons. One, it helped the attendance to have Michigan State come to Michigan and play the games and sell more tickets, but also state political pressure, like these are kind of the two biggest schools in the state and the politicians want them to play each other."Michigan attempted to block Michigan State as the tenth Big Ten team"Michigan State immediately wanted to get what is now an open spot here in the Big Ten... Michigan State's case was that it was the largest state-supported institution of the Big Ten states that wasn't in the conference. It felt like that they had everything in place. "The Big Ten was the premier conference outside of the Ivy League out in the East. And John Hannah, the president of Michigan State, knew this was the moment for Michigan State to take that step forward. If they could get into the Big Ten conference with all these prestigious state schools, that would elevate Michigan State finally, to the level that they had long wanted to be at."Michigan State knew it would need help from somewhere else. And that turned out to be Minnesota. Minnesota had a beef with Michigan because Michigan had alleged that Minnesota had committed some sort of violations... and Purdue was in a similar boat. So you had a couple of schools in there conference who were sort of upset with Michigan throwing its weight around and feeling like it ran the conference. And one of the ways some of the schools felt like they could push back on that was to bring Michigan State into the conference."Is Ohio State the bigger rival for Michigan? Chris says yes."I think for Michigan fans, the biggest rivalry they look at is Ohio State. And for Michigan State fans, the one they look at most is Michigan. That makes it a little bit awkward. "The way I've always looked at it is that... I think Michigan wants to beat Ohio State more, but they don't want to lose to Michigan State more. That's the loss that hurts more because you have to hear about it every day at lunch, at the water cooler for the next 365 days. That's part of the rivalry."

articles.content: I’m calling it: time of death, November 6th, 1:30 AM, by tweet. Elon Musk’s declaration Friday that Tesla would be “winding down” production of the Cybertruck next year to make room for the Cybercab was fascinating for a number of reasons. First, it was a humiliating way to kill a vehicle that was once hailed as the pinnacle of Tesla’s engineering — faster than a Porsche 911, more powerful than an F-150, able to leap over the Model Y as a singular representation of Musk’s Blade Runner-inspired designs for the future. “I think the Tesla Cybertruck is our best product ever,” he declared during a 2019 earnings call. (He prefaced the statement by saying, “This could be totally wrong. I could be totally out to lunch here.” It would appear so!) The fact that Musk would just quietly put an end to the Cybertruck without any fanfare was a sign of how far it had fallen, not just in the eyes of the public, but in the eyes of its creator, the man most responsible for brute-forcing this low-emission, low-poly technological nightmare into the world. Tesla actually thought the Cybertruck would be a huge hit, targeting production and demand of 250,000 units per year. To date, the company has only sold 70,000 units — total. Musk’s other company, SpaceX, ended up being one of the largest single purchasers of Cybertrucks to absorb unsold inventory. Musk had to become his own customer to make the Cybertruck look better on paper. But the death of the Cybertruck is even more noteworthy given the timing of Musk’s tweet, coming just three days after his epic flop at the ballot box. Musk poured over $445 million into Republican races, with most of his money targeting his home turf of Texas — headquarters to both Tesla and SpaceX. Between funnels of $168 million to super PACs backing Republican Senate candidate Ken Paxton and nearly $35 million redirected from his own America PAC, Musk dropped more than $200 million on the Lone Star State alone. All that money, and zero return. Democrat James Talarico crushed Paxton by 12 points to break a 38-year Democratic Senate drought, while Gina Hinojosa ousted Greg Abbott from the governor’s mansion. Texas turned blue, despite the best efforts of the world’s richest man — or perhaps because of them? Americans are fed up: they don’t want Musk meddling in their government, and they especially don’t want his stainless-steel monument to his own vanity and utter refusal to accept human feedback. The Cybertruck was one of the most epic failures in modern automotive history. While it succeeded as a viral PR spectacle and initially became a top-selling premium electric pickup in early 2024, it ultimately collapsed under the weight of Musk’s own hubris. The reasons for the Cybertruck’s failures are almost too many to enumerate: too expensive, not as much range or towing power as promised, too many recalls, and, well, it looked the way it did. But when Musk outed himself as a Trump supporter, forever tying himself to Trump’s MAGA brand, the Cybertruck went with him. Electric vehicles are typically associated with a style of coastal progressivism, but the Cybertruck crossed the aisle to become a physical avatar of Trump’s ugly brand of politics. And more so than any other car in modern history, the Cybertruck was inseparable from its creator. By the time Musk threw hundreds of millions of dollars into Trump’s campaign, launched the America PAC, and took a prominent position in Trump’s administration as the head of the disastrous DOGE project, owning a Cybertruck had become a rolling liability. People who owned a Model 3 or Model Y could credibly claim they bought it before “Elon went crazy,” as the bumper stickers would later declare — a Cybertruck owner could make no such claim. To be sure, most people who bought Cybertrucks were not interested in distancing themselves from Musk’s brand of trollish politics. A big part of MAGA culture is owning the libs. And because liberals, car purists, and environmentalists couldn’t stand the Cybertruck — mocking everything from its sharp edges to its build quality — buying one became a way to get under their skin. Before long, people were slapping Trump wraps on them, flying flags from the truck beds, and turning them into props for conservative rallies. But vibes shift, as they always do. Edgelords lose their edge, and voters become weary and wary of efforts to divide them. The blue tsunami was a historic rejection of Trump and Musk’s brand of right-wing grievance politics. When the spectacle wore off, the bluster stopped feeling like rebellion and started looking like a shit way to run a government. In a single election, the country said it was done. The results on Tuesday also rendered the Cybertruck an instant relic. The election stripped away the sheen of inevitability that once insulated both the billionaire and his pet project. It’s a relief, but a peculiar one at that. Has there ever been a vehicle so desperate to look like the future, only to become an immediate symbol of the past?

articles.description: House Democrats will start their majority focused on boosting healthcare and ending the Iran war AP News Sunday shows preview: Democrats lay out legislative agenda; Congress leadership sparks infighting The Hill Democrats prepare for something new in the House: Teamwork Politico Five ways the midterm election results could reshape Donald Trump’s America The Globe and Mail Midterm power shift sets up new policy battle
articles.content: WASHINGTON (AP) — House Democratic leaders are placing an early emphasis on healthcare as they discuss their immediate priorities upon the swearing-in of the new Congress on Jan. 3. Early votes in the House next year are expected to focus on boosting Medicaid and restoring an enhanced tax subsidy that is designed to lower the cost of Affordable Care Act health plans for millions of enrollees. Democrats are also promising swift action on legislation to stop the war with Iran and to reverse some of President Donald Trump’strade tariffs. “We’re going to get out of the gate fast,” said New York Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, the Democratic leader who is in line to become the next House speaker. The legislative flurry carries enormous stakes for Democrats as they seek to translate their sweeping victories in the midterms — their numbers will exceed 250 in the 435-member House — into achievements that deliver on their promises to lower the cost of living. The Capitol is seen under gray skies after American voters this week flipped control of both chambers of Congress from Republican control to the Democrats, in Washington, Friday, Nov. 6, 2026. (AP Photo/J. Scott Applewhite) The Capitol is seen under gray skies after American voters this week flipped control of both chambers of Congress from Republican control to the Democrats, in Washington, Friday, Nov. 6, 2026. (AP Photo/J. Scott Applewhite) Passing those bills should not be a problem with such a large Democratic House majority. Getting them signed into law most certainly could be. A 60-vote threshold in the Senate looms for the legislation, as does a potential presidential veto. Trump on election night posted a photo on his social media site of a red hat with a simple message on it: “VETO”. Following those early votes, Jeffries said five working groups are developing plans to put forward bills that would lower costs in areas such as housing, energy, groceries and caregiving. Rep. Ted Lieu, D-Calif., said Democrats will at some point take up legislation dealing with artificial intelligence and data centers. He is part of a group of lawmakers working on a document that will lay out some of the priorities for Jeffries to consider. “House Republicans last year made a conscious decision to let the AI industry run wild, and that was a bad decision politically and a bad decision on policy,” Lieu said. “Two things will change next term. We will hold public hearings on AI. We will pass legislation, reasonable guardrails on AI, and specifically data centers.” A CleanSpark Bitcoin mining center is seen on Sept. 4, 2026, in Dalton, Ga. (AP Photo/Mike Stewart, File) A CleanSpark Bitcoin mining center is seen on Sept. 4, 2026, in Dalton, Ga. (AP Photo/Mike Stewart, File) Democrats are trying to reverse Medicaid changes that are expected to cut more than $900 billion from the program over a decade. The Republican-approved cuts helped offset some of the costs of Trump’s big tax and spending cut bill that was signed into law last year. The Medicaid changes in the bill imposed new administrative requirements and added conditions for eligibility, including work requirements. Some of the most substantial changes have yet to take effect. Still, enrollment in Medicaid has dropped by about 5 million, or about 7% since July 2025, when the bill was signed into law, according to KFF, a health policy research and news organization. Reversing those cuts would likely require Trump and the Republicans to abandon the hard-fought changes they made to cut entitlement spending in their signature tax bill. It’s an unlikely proposition. The effort to extend enhanced tax subsidies for certain enrollees in ACA plans has also been debated and voted on in the current Congress. The measure passed the House with some Republican support but stalled in the Senate. There also have been numerous war powers votes regarding Iran — 14 in the Senate and six in the House. Demonstrators chant slogans as one holds a portrait of the Iranian Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei during a pro-government gathering in Tehran, Iran, Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026. (AP Photo/Vahid Salemi) Demonstrators chant slogans as one holds a portrait of the Iranian Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei during a pro-government gathering in Tehran, Iran, Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026. (AP Photo/Vahid Salemi) Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., said going into the election that a Democratic majority in the next Congress would amount to “two years of paralysis.” “I don’t think that’s good for anybody,” Thune said. But Democratic leader Chuck Schumer of New York is insisting that Democrats will push their agenda with or without the Republican president’s help. “If he vetoes it, it will show the divisions. As much as we didn’t want to shut down, when we shut down the government for a month over healthcare, people knew we were on their side,” Schumer said in an interview with The New York Times’ podcast “The Daily.” Schumer said he believes Democrats can gain some Republican votes on restoring the enhanced subsidies for ACA plans. When asked if he was hearing from Republicans expressing a willingness to work with him on legislation, he replied: “They’re never so definitive but, yes, I am getting initial signs that way on certain issues, not on every issue.” While the prospects for getting any of the early priority bills over the finish line are uncertain, the votes in Congress will help frame the choices voters will face during a presidential election in 2028. Progressive groups call the agenda outlined by Jeffries a good early start, but they have much greater expectations for Democrats this Congress. “It’s perfectly fine if the Senate and the House are unified and Donald Trump is standing in the way because that sets up another tidal wave election in 2028,” said Adam Green, co-founder of the Progressive Change Campaign Committee, a Democratic-aligned group that backs progressive candidates and policies. At the same time, he said Schumer cannot be content to let bills die in the Senate because of the 60-vote threshold. “It will require the Democrats to get rid of the filibuster,” Green said. “There’s no doubt about it.” He said there’s a disparity because Republicans’ top priorities — tax cuts and Supreme Court justices — can get through with simple majorities. But the Democratic Party’s top priorities require 60 votes to overcome a filibuster. “The only question is will the American public trust Democrats enough to keep giving us more power or will this week’s gains whittle away because we do nothing? That’s why the filibuster is a threshold question,” Green said. Schumer in an interview with The Associated Press this week would not say whether he would try and eliminate the filibuster. “The focus has got to be on getting things done,” Schumer said. “That’s all I am saying.” In a memo to fellow members of the Congressional Progressive Caucus, Rep. Greg Casar, D-Texas, said Democrats also need to target what he called “powerful forces outside of government.” Examples he cited were corporations using Americans’ private data to adjust their pricing based on a consumer’s personal data and AI companies that he says are putting jobs and lives at risk. “By focusing not just on the Trump administration but also on big corporations and billionaires, we will show the American people we are not just anti-Trump but also pro-worker and pro-consumer,” Casar said. Associated Press writer Mary Clare Jalonick contributed to this report.

Commentary: The true guardians of our democracy
articles.description: As the dust settles on the 2026 blue wave tsunami of a national election, the predictable wave of political analysis and backslapping has begun.
