Here in Michigan and across the country, an important story of this election isn’t just […]
articles.content: Election workers collect absentee ballots outside the Department of Elections in Detroit on Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Janelle D. James/Michigan Advance)As the dust settles on the 2026 blue wave tsunami of a national election, the predictable wave of political analysis and backslapping has begun. Pundits and the political class will spend weeks dissecting voter shifts, messaging strategies and polling margins. Here in Michigan and across the country, an important story of this election isn’t just about who won or lost. It is about how the election was run: smoothly, securely, and with an unwavering commitment to the fair and transparent democratic process. For that, we must thank our secretary of state, now governor-elect, Jocelyn Benson and her exceptional team, as well as municipal clerks, poll workers and precinct volunteers across America — and specifically here in Michigan — who managed the logistical marvel of our vital voting system. This year’s success was also fortified by an extraordinary, collaborative effort that took place far outside the standard political arenas. To truly appreciate why our system held strong, we must also thank former Democratic Gov. Jim Blanchard, who served as ambassador and was my former boss; former Republican Gov. John Engler; former Republican U.S. Rep. and state Senate Majority Leader Michael Bishop; and former Lt. Gov. John Cherry, a Democrat. and the leaders of the Detroit Regional Chamber. In an era deeply fractured by political tribalism, these bipartisan leaders showed our state—and the country—a master class in pragmatic statesmanship. As leaders of the bipartisan Democracy Defense Foundation in Michigan, these former political rivals chose to stand shoulder to shoulder in defense of our democracy. Rather than retreating into comfortable partisanship, they put their collective weight behind a singular, vital mission: upholding public trust in our election infrastructure and protecting the integrity of the vote. Throughout the campaign cycle, they traveled the state, hosting forums, speaking with the media, and utilizing new polling to directly address and de-escalate public anxieties surrounding voter safety and ballot security. Their message was simple yet profound: Our election systems are decentralized, heavily scrutinized and robustly protected by our own neighbors. By auditing the facts and calling for civic responsibility, they helped lower the temperature of the public discourse. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE They reminded us that while we can disagree passionately about policy, we must remain unified in our respect for the democratic process. Crucially, this message found a powerful amplifier in the Michigan business community, spearheaded by the Detroit Regional Chamber. Under the leadership of longtime President and CEO Sandy Baruah and his outstanding team, the business sector recognized that a stable democracy is the literal bedrock of a strong state and prosperous economy. The chamber did not sit on the sidelines. Instead, it mobilized its expansive network to transform corporate civic engagement into a tangible, frontline reality. Through focused election briefings and executive webinars, the chamber consistently educated regional leaders on the extensive, multi-layered safeguards built into Michigan’s voting framework. More importantly, it issued a direct call to action for employers. Jointly they prodded chamber members and the citizens of Michigan to move beyond passive observation and actively encourage their workforces to serve as local poll workers and precinct watchers. The business community responded in kind. By providing employees with the flexibility, and in some cases dedicated time off, to work the polls, regional employers helped solve a critical staffing puzzle for local clerks. The result of this combined effort was palpable on Election Day. Because of the infrastructure championed by our local clerks, reinforced by the structural support of the chamber and the bipartisan shield, our precincts operated with transparent efficiency. Voters stood in lines managed by well-trained volunteers, ballots were counted meticulously, and the system functioned exactly as it was designed to do. Democracy is not a self-sustaining machine; it requires continuous care, human labor, and a shared cultural agreement that the rules matter. This November, Michigan and America proved that when political rivals lock arms and the business community and others align their collective resources with civic duty, we can withstand the forces of lies and cynicism. To the thousands of election workers who checked IDs and handed out “I Voted” stickers, we thank you. And to Jim Blanchard, John Engler, former Rep. Michael Bishop, former Lt. Gov John Cherry and the Detroit Regional Chamber, thank you for reminding us that defending our democracy is a job that belongs to all of us. You didn’t just protect an election; you strengthened the very fabric of our state and nation.

articles.title: What's next for Michigan Democrats after winning a state government trifecta?
articles.description: Gongwer's Zach Gorchow joins Morning Edition to discuss swing districts, strategy in a lame-duck session, and when an election victory is actually a mandate.
articles.content: (Lester Graham / Michigan Radio)The blue wave of the 2026 election is reshaping the power balance in Michigan state politics for 2027 and beyond. Democrats will retain control of the governor's office, have won a larger majority in the state Senate, and are set to regain control of the state House.For more on the election and its implications at the state Capitol, Michigan Public Morning Edition host Doug Tribou spoke with Gongwer News Service President Zach Gorchow.Doug Tribou: All 110 state House seats were on the ballot this election, and Democrats were able to regain the majority they lost two years ago. They also not only retained their majority in the state Senate, but expanded it. What were some of the key races that stood out to you in this cycle?Zach Gorchow: I think what stands out is that the Democrats essentially won every single contested race and then a couple that weren't even really seriously contested. I mean, this was a complete sweep. You know, we don't have these happen that often. But we certainly had it happen on Tuesday. You could look at the traditionally competitive districts, places like Battle Creek's district. That is sort of your prototypical swing district. It flips back and forth often, and it went to the Democrats this time. No surprise. Areas that are emerging Democratic territory, that have been trending Democratic, like Rochester and Rochester Hills, Holland, those went Democratic. Areas that had been trending Republican in the Trump era, seats that Republicans had flipped away from Democrats Downriver, places like suburban Genesee County, those flipped back to the Democrats. So there's really not one simple way to look at this. This was sort of an all-of-the-above situation.DT: What are some of the policy agendas that you think Democrats are likely to focus on as they consolidate power in Lansing?ZG: One, we know that Governor-elect Benson has said the first legislation she would like to sign would be a state Voting Rights Act. I would expect that the incoming Democratic Legislature will be very amenable to that. Benson has also talked about dealing with costs and affordability. She talked about some targeted tax breaks like a caregiver tax credit. So I would certainly expect we're going to see something along those lines, too. But I think the other place to really look is to the last time Democrats had complete control in the 2023-2024 term and the items that a lot of Democrats wished they had gotten done that term that I think are going to get dusted off.DT: Well, as you mentioned, many Democratic supporters viewed that period, that 2023-2024 session, as a squandered opportunity in terms of the amount of significant legislation that wound up being passed. So it sounds like you think Democrats will have more ability to get more done this time around?ZG: Oh, for sure. I mean, that last term in '23, '24, they had bare minimum majorities: 56-54 in the House and 20-18 in the Senate. That meant in the House, they needed every Democrat to vote for something in order to pass it, because in most cases, the Republicans weren't coming on board. And for all intents and purposes, it was the same situation in the Senate, too. That's really difficult. Now, the Democrats don't need every single member to pass something. You know, there was a joke in the last term in the House. You had effectively 56 Speakers of the House because you couldn't lose a single vote. So they could exert an incredible amount of leverage to get their vote on any one bill.DT: Now that the election is behind us, mostly, and Democrats are set to have full control again in Lansing, we've entered the lame-duck period between now and January. And we still have a divided government with a Democratic majority in the Senate and a Republican majority in the House. Do you expect them to pass much legislation before the session ends?ZG: I don't. The Democrats really have no incentive to work with the Republicans in the House on anything really significant, because why would you compromise with the House Republicans when you're going to have full control in a couple of months? And if you're the House Republicans, you know, what incentive do you really have to try to move much knowing that the Democrats are likely to say, “Thanks, but no thanks.”Now, that being said, I would expect some bills to get to the governor's desk. But these are going to be kind of what we call cat-and-dogs kinds of bills around Lansing. Smaller potatoes, non-controversial, probably some things that legislators who are not returning next session would like to get done before their careers end. There's no indication that outgoing Governor (Gretchen) Whitmer has any big asks or anything big she wants to get done before she leaves. So there just doesn't seem to be a lot of impetus for anything significant.DT: One of the things that fascinates me about politics is that on the national and the state level, regardless of party or political persuasion, when one party wins decisively in the legislative branch or in an executive office like the president or the governor, it's often not long before the newly elected officials sort of buy into the idea that the entire voting populace has given them a mandate. And then it's not long before they step beyond what people are expecting or step outside of some of the core issues that fueled their success, which in turns sets them up for sometimes failure or diminished returns in the next election cycle. And at the federal level this time around, it's easy to see how there might be a congressional mandate here for the newly elected members of the House and Senate. But here in Michigan, Democrats already had a lot of power. They had the governor's office, they had the attorney general, the secretary of state. They had a majority in the Senate. Is it trickier for them to figure out the priorities, even though they just had decisive victories here in Michigan?ZG: This is sort of a tale as old as time, you know. When you win elections, the state level and a sweep like this, and this has been true of Democrats and Republicans. Some would say sometimes that these trifecta governments maybe go too far or exceed what voters were expecting. But Governor (John) Engler once said something like, "change is the mandate." And I think one could say that in 2024, the Republicans won everything nationally and in Michigan, almost everything in Michigan, largely because voters were so angry about inflation and how expensive things were. President (Joe) Biden and Democrats paid a steep price in 2024 for not addressing those issues. And President (Donald) Trump and the Republicans paid a steep price in 2026 for not addressing those issues. If the Democrats in Michigan end up focusing more on core Democratic priorities and don't try to do some things to provide some relief to people, whatever form that looks like, I think they'll pay a price. And, you know, that could be true at the federal level, too.Editor's note: Some quotes in this article have been lightly edited for length and clarity. You can play the full audio of the interview near the top of this page.

articles.title: DTE to sell non-utility business to fund grid upgrades, data center growth
articles.description: The DTE Vantage sale does not include EES Coke Battery on Zug Island, a facility for which DTE is appealing a $100 million fine for air pollution.
articles.content: DTE Energy announced Thursday that it’s selling its non-utility DTE Vantage business to help fund infrastructure investments needed to strengthen the grid, build renewables, and accommodate data centers. This story also appeared in Planet Detroit DTE expects to finalize an agreement for an additional 2 gigawatt, hyperscale data center by the end of the year, and the utility has 5-6 GW of total data center capacity in its pipeline, President and CEO Joi Harris said during a Thursday earnings call. One gigawatt is roughly the amount of power used by 800,000 homes. Data center growth is providing a “once-in-a-generation” investment opportunity for the company, Harris said. The utility plans to invest $44 billion over the next five years to improve reliability, transition to cleaner energy, and meet new data center demand growth, she said. DTE’s five-year plan includes building 7.6 GW of new solar and wind generation, 2.1 GW of natural gas generation, and 2.7 GW of energy storage. The utility reported $481 million in third-quarter operating earnings. Annual earnings per share growth is expected to increase from 6%-8% this year to more than 9% in 2028, Harris said. DTE’s data center contracts Critics of DTE’s contracts for Oracle and OpenAI’s data center in Saline Township and Google’s data center in Van Buren Township have objected to potential climate, environmental, and ratepayer impacts. Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel filed a petition for a rehearing Oct. 30 following the Michigan Public Service Commission’s approval of DTE’s contracts for the Google data center. Nessel said the MPSC order has a “litany of errors,” and creates an unnecessary risk of cost-shifting from DTE and Google to other customers. Harris said data centers will create “meaningful affordability benefits” for customers, allowing DTE to sell excess capacity and spread fixed costs across a larger customer base. The Oracle and OpenAI project will allow DTE to refrain from filing additional rate hike requests until 2028, and the Google data center will potentially allow DTE to further delay new filings, the CEO said. DTE requested a $474.3 million electric rate hike in April, saying it could pause rate hike requests for at least two years if the utility secures a “constructive” outcome in the rate case and the Saline Township data center comes online by the end of 2027. DTE CEO expects ratemaking legislation In response to a question about this week’s midterm election, Harris said she anticipates the next Michigan Legislature will take up bills to make ratemaking a multiyear process. Democrats regained control of the Michigan House following Tuesday’s vote and maintained control of the state Senate and governor’s office. The MPSC recommended in August that lawmakers introduce legislation to allow the commission to set multiyear rate plans to help Michiganders plan for more consistent utility bills. “We’re continuing to work on making sure that there’s a constructive outcome, that we’re influencing the thinking of the MPSC, and certainly preparing to educate the legislators that are new to this policy framework along the way,” Harris said. DTE’s Zug Island facility excluded from Vantage sale DTE’s sale of its Vantage business is expected to close in the first half of 2027 and raise $3 billion, which will help DTE invest in utility infrastructure, and reduce the company’s need for debt and equity financing, Harris said. DTE Vantage is a subsidiary of DTE Energy that provides non-utility energy services for commercial and industrial customers. Douglas Jester, a consultant with 5 Lakes Energy, told Planet Detroit that DTE’s sale of Vantage will allow DTE to meet the growing need for investment without diluting the value of its stock. Data centers, Michigan’s renewable energy requirements, and grid improvements are all increasing the pace of investments DTE needs to make, he said. Without selling Vantage, DTE would need to issue more debt and stock to fund these investments, which would dilute the value of its stock, Jester said. Dilution lowers the earnings per share and can lower stock prices. A DTE spokesperson told Planet Detroit the Vantage sale will enable the company to make significant investments in its utilities, benefiting homes and businesses. “Our agreements with data center customers ensure they will cover all new costs required to serve them,” the spokesperson said. Harris said the Vantage sale will include the sale of all the subsidiary’s assets — except EES Coke Battery on Zug Island. In February, a federal judge ordered the utility and subsidiaries including EES Coke to pay a $100 million fine, comply with federal air quality rules, and pay for $20 million in community air quality improvements due to Clean Air Act violations. DTE appealed the judgement to the Sixth Circuit Court of Appeals in March. “Nothing EES Coke did warrants the largest stationary-source penalty in the CAA’s history,” DTE lawyers wrote in an October court filing, referring to the Clean Air Act. This article first appeared on Planet Detroit and is republished here under a Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial 4.0 International License.

articles.title: Why a new report on Anthropic automating AI development is alarming researchers
articles.description: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei. | Photo: Jason Henry/Bloomberg via Getty Images Anthropic is using AI to build more powerful AI. And it appears to be working remarkably well, with the company's models improving roughly twice as quickly as a year ago, with little indication of slowing down. That's according to a new report published Thursday by the AI safety research organization METR, following an 11-week investigation i
articles.content: Anthropic is using AI to build more powerful AI. And it appears to be working remarkably well, with the company’s models improving roughly twice as quickly as a year ago, with little indication of slowing down. That’s according to a new report published Thursday by the AI safety research organization METR, following an 11-week investigation inside the company, as part of a report evaluating its AI research and development. The probe is separate from a program offering safety researchers “employee-like” access to systems in the wake of high-profile hacking incidents over the summer. The findings offer some of the clearest evidence yet of AI accelerating its own development, raising questions about how quickly the technology could advance toward a future in which AI systems can improve themselves with little or no human involvement. They also come at a pivotal time for Anthropic, which is preparing to go public even as its CEO, Dario Amodei, has publicly called for labs to pump the brakes on AI development. But while the report offers a rare glimpse into the inner workings of the world’s leading AI labs, what it leaves out is just as revealing. Anthropic was permitted to redact portions of the final report as part of its agreement with METR, and it appears to have exercised that power liberally, raising questions about how much the public really knows about the pace — and risks — of frontier AI development. Here are some of the biggest takeaways. AI is dramatically accelerating Anthropic’s research and development One of METR’s most noteworthy findings is that Anthropic’s AI models are improving roughly twice as quickly as they were a year ago, with benchmark scores suggesting “that Anthropic has made roughly two years of historical progress over the last year.” Crucially, METR’s researchers said they “are confident” that the acceleration was not simply due to scaling up the computing power used to train the models, which historically has been a major driver of AI progress. Instead, the researchers said that the majority of the acceleration as of October “is due to AI,” with its contribution growing over time. That finding was supported by informal Slack polls and interviews with Anthropic employees, which pointed to sizable productivity gains. METR wrote that employees using Anthropic’s most capable internal model on average self-reported being around 12 times as productive at their respective work as they would have been without AI assistance, around double what staff had reported just a few months earlier while using Mythos 5. [Image: METR’s report includes this graphic showing Anthropic employees’ responses to Slack polls about AI speeding up their work. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/11/self-reported-uplift.png?quality=90&strip=all] For now, much of that acceleration appears to be coming from AI assisting human researchers, rather than AI working independently, though METR warned that “there are some signs that fully autonomous contributions will play a larger role soon.” Notably, the researchers said they found no clear signs of diminishing returns or observable bottlenecks that could prevent “even faster acceleration.” Three of Anthropic’s newest AI models remain under wraps Anthropic’s researchers are using more advanced AI models than the rest of us, with a lot of the acceleration and productivity gains described by METR attributable to unreleased internal models. Over the past six months, Anthropic has finished training three models it has yet to release, according to METR. The pace of development is swift, with the models — codenamed Model 2, Model 3, and Model 4 — completing training in July, August-September, and September-October, respectively. METR also identified an unreleased model dating back to 2022, called Unreleased 2022. “These are the codenames shared with us; we understand they have different internal codenames,” the researchers wrote. Anthropic is keeping key information secret Anthropic gave METR access to a host of non-public information, including confidential research, model performance data, and employee interviews as part of the research process. It had no obligation to do so and by METR’s own admission, the AI lab “shared more information than was initially scoped for this project, surpassing our expectations.” This is commendable, but it is worth noting that Anthropic did not grant researchers unrestricted access, nor the kind of “employee-like” access it has promised other METR safety researchers as part of a separate program announced last month. It is an important distinction, given the reputational benefits companies can gain from independent assessments, even when they come with significant restrictions. And there were significant restrictions. Anthropic had the power to redact information from METR’s final report — and it used that power extensively. “We submitted a ~100-page full report on our assessment to Anthropic. For the public version, Anthropic redacted a majority of the evidence we found most informative,” METR wrote on X. METR reiterated those concerns throughout the report, highlighting other limitations on its access. “Our pipeline of information was relatively narrow, and a small number of our requests for data were denied.” METR repeatedly stressed the impact Anthropic’s redaction decisions had on its ability to communicate its findings and for others to assess what’s going on at the company. It noted that much of the redacted evidence could have “multiple plausible interpretations,” making it difficult for the public to assess its findings, understand the uncertainties surrounding them, and judge the evidence themselves. “As a consequence [of the redactions], the public has to rely on METR’s judgment much more than would be ideal, given the weight of the questions answered here,” the report said. [Media: https://twitter.com/Sam_McCandlish/status/2118422266669371519] In the report, METR said Anthropic justified the redactions on the grounds that releasing the information could benefit its rivals. However, METR said “most of the redacted information was very high-level,” even though it said it was not in position to comment whether redactions were justified commercially or not. “We redacted a lot, and I accept that this makes it harder for others to check METR’s work,” Anthropic cofounder Sam McCandlish acknowledged in a lengthy post on X responding to METR’s findings. “But we determined that sharing exactly what is driving the speedup isn’t the right thing to do, both because it’s commercially sensitive and because it risks handing out a roadmap for others to go faster,” he said, adding that doing so would make the risks METR is concerned about “worse.” McCandlish said that it’s a trade-off, but maintained Anthropic had made the “right call” in deciding to redact the information. He said the company plans to publish its own report on the speed of AI progress “in the coming weeks,” as well as new steps it’s taking to strengthen safety. Anthropic is accelerating the very technology it warns is dangerous and faster than many expected The publication of METR’s report has provoked a fierce backlash among AI safety researchers and commentators, largely centered on an apparent contradiction at the heart of Anthropic’s approach to AI: The company has been one of the most outspoken advocates for safety and responsible development, yet the report suggests it is helping accelerate the technology toward a threshold many consider dangerous, while seemingly failing to live up to its own commitments to transparency and accountability. For some, the findings suggest that even many of the field’s most aggressive predictions about AI progress may be too conservative. They indicate that recursive self-improvement — AI systems that can autonomously develop increasingly powerful successor systems without human intervention, potentially accelerating development dramatically — may be closer than previously thought, raising concerns about whether existing safety measures can keep pace. While METR’s report only covers Anthropic, OpenAI said in September that it is “making strong progress” toward building an AI researcher that can “further progress on deep learning and alignment” by March 2028. Marius Hobbhahn, CEO and founder of Apollo Research, which conducts AI safety testing for several leading AI labs, told The Verge the report suggests a pace of AI-enabled research and development even faster than what was forecast in AI 2027, an influential scenario that envisions a key breakthrough toward self-improvement in early 2027. He said the report has attracted so much attention because it provides evidence about something that has been very hard to pin down: Just how quickly AI is accelerating its own development. Hobbhahn said the findings were broadly in line with what many in the field had expected, perhaps a little faster. Alan Chan, a senior research fellow at tech policy research center GovAI, told The Verge that the findings should prompt skeptics to reconsider their stance on AI accelerating AI development, and possibly shorten their timelines to when we will have systems that can fully automate tasks like software engineering. On X, other researchers commented on the rate of acceleration and its implications for AI development. Sydney Von Arx, founder and CEO of AI safety organization The Nightingale Collective and a former METR researcher, also compared the findings to AI 2027’s timeline. Ryan Greenblatt, a METR researcher formerly of AI safety organization Redwood Research and one of three external researchers permitted to investigate OpenAI’s hack of Hugging Face, said he “was seriously wrong about RSI speed up; I previously expected much less in 2026.” Frustration is mounting over Anthropic’s approach to safety Beyond highlighting the speed of AI development, the report has also fueled a growing sense of frustration over Anthropic’s role in driving that progress. The company has been one of the most vocal proponents of responsible AI development — and no stranger to calling for others to slow down — yet appears to be racing ahead itself. This report only builds on already heightened tensions from its IPO prospectus and future plans released last month. Anthropic’s decision to heavily redact the report, citing grounds that revealing more could help its rivals accelerate their own development, has fueled accusations of hypocrisy. Daniel Kokotajlo, a former OpenAI researcher who now runs the AI Futures Project, which published AI 2027, accused Anthropic of “recklessly gambling with our lives,” adding that “it is pretty rich” of the company to cite others going faster as a reason to redact information when it does “not appear to be slowing down much at all.” Anthropic declined to answer The Verge’s questions about the report and ensuing criticism, instead directing us to McCandlish’s post. The redactions have also renewed calls for greater transparency and independent oversight of frontier AI labs, which grew to new heights earlier this year following a spate of incidents involving rogue AI agents. Brianna Rosen, research director for frontier security at the Institute for AI Policy and Strategy, told The Verge that it was concerning that companies, not governments, were effectively calling the shots on automating AI research. “For democratic oversight to work, independent evaluators need the freedom to explain why they reached their conclusions, governments need to assess the evidence themselves, and the public has to trust this process,” Rosen said. “The report was not sufficiently transparent about the evidence.” Pressure is building for more transparency from AI labs Hobbhahn echoed Rosen’s concerns, saying that much of the reaction to the report stems from the apparent gap between Anthropic’s public safety stance and its actions. He pointed to the company’s decision to cancel part of the assessment de

articles.title: The Bantu expansion changed Africa. Scientists are still tracing how.
articles.description: Genes and archaeology are revealing how Bantu speakers spread across much of Africa.
articles.content: It’s not easy to extract iron from its ore. But the peoples of the ancient city of Great Zimbabwe—the capital of a thriving kingdom in southern Africa between 1000 to 1700 AD—were masters. At sites near the city’s stone ruins, clusters of iron-smelting furnaces survive today as mounds of rubble. At Mashava, a village 25 miles northwest, fragments bear fingermarks of those who long ago smoothed the structures’ clay interiors. Some of the furnaces were nearly an adult’s arm span in width, with walls thick and strong to contain the heat of more than 2,100° Fahrenheit needed to smelt iron. Unlike other furnaces that required workers to force air into them with bellows, these were designed to suck air in, then out through a chimney, no human labor required. This would have made it significantly easier to produce the iron, which was fashioned into hoes, axes, and arrowheads.Read full article Comments

articles.title: Democratic wins put Medicaid expansion back in play in holdout states
articles.description: In a handful of holdout states, Democrats appear ready to use their newly won statehouse dominance to expand Medicaid under the Affordable Care Act. In at least four states — Georgia, Kansas, Texas and Wisconsin — the midterm election results have tilted the political calculus toward expansion, though lawmakers have yet to lay out details. […]
articles.content: Georgia Democratic Gov.-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms celebrates her victory on Nov. 3 in Atlanta. Bottoms made full Medicaid expansion central to her campaign and has called it “a day one priority.” Democratic victories could bring Medicaid expansion to a handful of other states. (Photo by Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder)In a handful of holdout states, Democrats appear ready to use their newly won statehouse dominance to expand Medicaid under the Affordable Care Act. In at least four states — Georgia, Kansas, Texas and Wisconsin — the midterm election results have tilted the political calculus toward expansion, though lawmakers have yet to lay out details. Medicaid is the joint federal-state insurance program for people with low incomes. Georgia and Wisconsin have limited expansion programs, but neither has approved the broader expansion allowed under the Affordable Care Act. “Before Tuesday, I wouldn’t have expected much activity in the 10 remaining states that have not expanded Medicaid” to more adults under the Affordable Care Act, said Larry Levitt, executive vice president for health policy at the health research and policy nonprofit KFF, on a media call after the election. “But I think that dynamic has changed.” Under the Affordable Care Act, better known as Obamacare, states can expand Medicaid to cover adults earning up to 138% of the federal poverty line — about $22,000 a year for a single person — and the federal government will pick up 90% of the costs for those newly eligible enrollees. Forty states took the deal, adding nearly 20 million people with low incomes to the rolls. In the remaining 10 states, which have been mostly controlled by Republicans, expansion has been blocked by GOP opponents who think it is too expensive or who are ideologically opposed to growing government programs. Georgia Democratic Gov.-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms made full Medicaid expansion central to her campaign and has called it “a day one priority.” “This is thrilling for me because this is the reason I ran for office in the first place,” said Dr. Michelle Au, a Democratic Georgia state representative and physician. In Georgia, Democrats won every statewide office that was on the ballot and appear poised to take control of the state House, though Republicans will still control the state Senate. Democrats would need bipartisan support to get expansion passed. “We are going to see a bill and it’s going to be an interesting process in the newly divided government,” said Au. She said a 2024 Medicaid expansion bill had bipartisan support among state legislators, including from Republicans representing rural districts facing hospital closures and higher rates of uninsured residents. The bill eventually died in committee, she said, in large part because it didn’t have the backing of Republican Gov. Brian Kemp. “What became apparent in that process was that there was nothing more important to the passage of this issue than having a strong governor who supports it,” Au said. “If anything, this issue has only gotten more urgent and popular” among voters, she said. Wisconsin’s new Democratic trifecta — the party will control both legislative chambers and the governor’s office — could make full Medicaid expansion much easier to pass. Wisconsin Democratic Gov.-elect David Crowley has deferred to legislators when asked about expansion. Democratic state Rep. Greta Neubauer, who is set to become House Speaker, stopped short of promising expansion in a call with reporters after the election. She said lawmakers will look at several options to address healthcare, reported the Wisconsin Examiner. Neubauer said Medicaid expansion was complicated by the Trump administration’s new work requirements and other changes to the program. “It’s a shame that Wisconsin has not done that up to this point,” she said. “We are going to be working very closely with the administration to figure out the best way to expand access to affordable healthcare for Wisconsinites, even given the Trump administration’s efforts to cut access and raise costs.” In July 2025, Trump signed a broad tax and spending measure that is projected to cut federal Medicaid spending by an estimated $886.8 billion over the next decade, largely because new work requirements will push people off the rolls, according to estimates by the Congressional Budget Office. The new rules, which will take effect in January, will apply to people who became eligible for Medicaid as a result of expansion. But the new Democratic-controlled Congress is expected to look at delaying or reversing the changes, which “may make it even more attractive for places like Texas and Georgia to try to expand,” Levitt said. Texas voters also voted Democrats into every statewide office that was on the ballot, including electing Democrat Gina Hinojosa as governor and flipping control of the state House. Republicans still control the state Senate. Hinojosa told a Houston television station that she would push the state legislature to expand Medicaid. Before the election, Kansas’ outgoing Democratic Gov. Laura Kelly called the Kansas’ Legislature’s refusal to expand Medicaid “the dumbest thing Kansas has ever done.” She said the main roadblock was opposition by Kansas’ Republican House Speaker. But this week, Kansas Democrats flipped as many as 20 seats in the Kansas House, quashing the Republican supermajority. Votes are still being tallied, but it appears that while Republicans will retain a majority in the state House and a supermajority in the state Senate, Democrat Cindy Holscher holds a narrow lead in the governor’s race. Holscher campaigned on promises of expanding Medicaid, saying Medicaid expansion would help prevent hospital closures and improve access to mental health services. She noted that expansion is popular across the state. “This is approved by, I believe, over 75% of the population,” she said. “This cuts across the political spectrum. Rural as well as urban areas say this is what we need to do.” Stateline reporter Anna Claire Vollers can be reached at avollers@stateline.org. articles.title: Latino voters singled out by top Democrat for credit in congressional victories
articles.description: WASHINGTON — The chair of the campaign arm for U.S. House Democrats said during a Friday press conference that this week’s midterm elections resulted in an overwhelming blue wave because of Latinos. Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee Chair Suzan DelBene said majorities won in the House and the Senate by Democrats couldn’t have happened without Latino voters. […]
articles.content: Voters line up to cast their ballots on the last day of early voting for the midterm election at the Pulaski County Regional Building in Little Rock, Arkansas on Monday, Nov. 2, 2026 (Photo by Ainsley Platt/Arkansas Advocate)WASHINGTON — The chair of the campaign arm for U.S. House Democrats said during a Friday press conference that this week’s midterm elections resulted in an overwhelming blue wave because of Latinos. Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee Chair Suzan DelBene said majorities won in the House and the Senate by Democrats couldn’t have happened without Latino voters. She said Democrats were only able to win competitive seats in Arizona, California, Colorado, Florida, Pennsylvania and Texas because of the Latino vote. While dozens of races are still too close to call, Democrats have won 253 seats, which is far past the 218 seats needed to control the majority in the lower chamber. Republicans have won 161 so far, according to The Associated Press. DelBene, a Washington state Democrat, said the president and his party broke their 2024 campaign promises when it came to lowering inflation and carrying out a mass deportation campaign of “the worst of the worst.” “They delivered the most anti-Latino agenda, defined by sky-high costs and out-of-control ICE operations,” she said, referring to U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents. DelBene said Democrats flipped 27 districts that President Donald Trump won in 2024 by double digits. She added that nearly all of her party’s Latino candidates won, with 54 Latinos who will be part of the 120th Congress in January, a historic number. Latinos who showed up during the midterm elections are “fed up” with inflation, high gas prices and the unpopular war in Iran, said Democratic Rep.-elect Johnny Garcia, who flipped a newly drawn Texas congressional district meant to favor a Republican candidate. “I knew I had to channel what the frustration was like here on the ground,” Garcia said. “Look, folks in this district, they just want to be able to go to HEB to buy their groceries, they want to be able to pay their utility bills with the wages they bring home,” he said. The Pew Research Center in October released a report that found that the economy was a top issue for Latinos. Elevation of Stephen Miller decried In the middle of the press conference, Trump separately announced that he would tap the architect of his mass deportation campaign, Stephen Miller, to serve as the White House chief of staff, and replace Trump’s longtime aide, Susie Wiles. She’s the highest-ranking official from the White House to leave after Tuesday’s election results. Elevating Miller to that role signals that the president is doubling down on his aggressive immigration crackdown that has generated an immense backlash across the country. Maria Teresa Kumar, who leads Voto Latino, said the decision to place Miller as White House chief of staff shows that “once again the Republicans are not reading the room.” Voto Latino is a nonprofit organization that aims to get young Latino and Hispanic people to register to vote and get politically involved. Kumar said the aggressive immigration crackdown by the Trump administration spurred young Latino voters, many of whom were voting for the first time, to head to the polls. “The fact that the president is putting Stephen Miller in that seat just speaks that he’s not learned his lesson,” she said.

articles.title: GOP Congress faces funding deadline, farm bill, lengthy to-do list in year-end session
articles.description: WASHINGTON — Voters may have given Democrats control of Congress in the midterm elections, but Republicans will remain in charge of both chambers during the lame-duck session that spans November and December. The relatively brief five-week schedule, which begins Monday, gives GOP leaders a chance to wrap up unfinished work before handing over power when […]
articles.content: The U.S. Capitol building in Washington, D.C., on Jan. 13, 2026. (Photo by Jennifer Shutt/States Newsroom)WASHINGTON — Voters may have given Democrats control of Congress in the midterm elections, but Republicans will remain in charge of both chambers during the lame-duck session that spans November and December. The relatively brief five-week schedule, which begins Monday, gives GOP leaders a chance to wrap up unfinished work before handing over power when the new session begins in early January. Congress could send the president several major pieces of legislation during that time, including the annual defense policy bill, the farm bill, a measure to regulate the college sports landscape and permitting reform to ease regulation on large construction projects. But lawmakers must pass a government funding bill before Dec. 11 to avoid another shutdown. Congress used a stopgap spending bill to keep federal programs up and running after the new fiscal year began Oct. 1. Democrats and Republicans don’t have enough time to broker bipartisan agreement on the dozen full-year appropriations bills, which will likely total around $1.9 trillion. That means lawmakers must use another stopgap spending bill to extend funding into next year, when Democrats will take the lead negotiating with President Donald Trump. North Dakota senator obstacle to confirmation push Senate Republicans are expected to use the rest of their time to confirm nominees before leaving for the holidays in mid-December. Democrats are unlikely to advance Trump’s nominees once they take over the Senate majority. A Senate GOP aide told States Newsroom that confirming judicial nominees will be a top priority in the coming session, in addition to funding the government, approving a farm bill and passing the annual defense policy bill. Sen. Kevin Cramer, however, continues to block confirmation of “any and all” of Trump’s nominees to pressure the administration to eliminate a President Joe Biden-era rule dealing with U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service wetland easements that the North Dakota Republican has said harm his state’s property owners. After FWS Director Brian Nesvik visited North Dakota in October, Cramer said he would release a few more of his holds, according to his office. Cramer has been willing to incrementally lift the holds based on progress he sees from the administration, allowing the confirmation of Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling. Cramer has also lifted a hold on Chris Klomp, nominee for deputy secretary of the Department of Health and Human Services. Overdue farm bill The farm bill, a substantial package of agriculture aid and nutrition programs, was supposed to become law years ago, but hasn’t amid long-running disagreements between the two parties. Senate Agriculture Committee Chairman John Boozman, R-Ark., said in a statement he hoped to finally reach a deal in the next few weeks, an accomplishment that will require support from Democrats. “Family farmers contending with numerous challenges to their viability cannot afford another Farm Bill delay,” he said. “Producers and rural communities are counting on us to deliver the predictability, certainty and support that a modernized Farm Bill provides. Congress has the opportunity to show them we understand how urgently they need these critical updates and I remain committed to helping get them signed into law this year.” The Senate Agriculture Committee approved its version of the farm bill in September but it didn’t garner bipartisan support. House Agriculture Committee Chairman Glenn “G.T.” Thompson, R-Pa., said in a statement that moving “a full, five-year farm bill across the finish line remains a top priority of mine as we look to the remaining legislative days of 2026. American producers and consumers cannot afford to wait any longer.” Minnesota Democratic Rep. Angie Craig, ranking member on the committee, said in a statement she remains “engaged in bipartisan, bicameral conversations” to address the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, allowing a gasoline blend with 15% ethanol and other priorities. “I remain deeply committed to addressing the unfunded SNAP mandate that Republicans forced onto states and counties,” she said. “Family farmers across the country are hurting right now and desperately want to see a farm bill that opens up domestic markets, like year-round E15, robustly funds conservation programs which are relied upon to boost farm income, and provides certainty for the next five years. I will continue to work with my colleagues to address these issues and more in the coming weeks.” Defense authorization, college sports bills Congress could reach a final deal on the massive defense policy bill, known as the National Defense Authorization Act, that lawmakers have approved annually for more than 60 years. House Armed Services Committee Chairman Mike Rogers, R-Ala., said in a statement that passing “the NDAA continues to be my highest priority, and I’m confident we can get this across the finish line.” “This legislation is crucial to our national security, and a failure to pass it would not only weaken American deterrence, but also abandon critical support for our men and women in uniform, including a pay raise and better access to healthcare and childcare,” he said. House Republican leadership will have to decide whether to put a college sports bill the Senate approved earlier this year up for a vote, a step its supporters say must happen this year. A spokesperson for the Senate Commerce, Science and Transportation Committee said in a statement there “is no realistic path to secure the same broad, bipartisan support for a new bill in 2027 and beyond. “Passing the Senate-approved bipartisan bill through the House and sending it to the President’s desk during the lame duck Congress gives House Republicans an opportunity to close out the 119th Congress with a significant win for President Trump, HBCUs, women’s sports, and student athletes,” the spokesperson wrote. “An attempt to amend it would be a surefire defeat for the colleges and fans counting on PCSA’s enactment.” House GOP leaders will also have to decide whether to debate and vote on a permitting reform bill that a bipartisan group of senators released in late September. The Senate is scheduled to take its first procedural vote on the legislation, which aims to speed construction of public projects by streamlining regulatory reviews, this week. GOP leadership shuffle and ethics overhaul In addition to work on legislation, the House could change its rules to address the various types of ethics violations that lawmakers engaged in during the last couple years. Florida Republican Rep. Kat Cammack and New Mexico Democratic Rep. Teresa Leger Fernández have worked together for months on a way to force better behavior. Off the floor, House Republicans will vote behind closed doors to decide who will lead them in the minority during the next Congress. Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., announced this week he will not seek to remain at the helm of the House GOP, setting up a race between Republican Leader Steve Scalise of Louisiana and Judiciary Committee Chairman Jim Jordan of Ohio. The other three congressional leaders — House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries, Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer and Senate Republican Leader John Thune — are all expected to remain in charge of their various conferences.

articles.title: $70 million gift excites Michigan tribal college, but funding gaps remain
articles.description: This story was originally published by Public News Service. A $70 million gift to the American Indian College Fund could help expand scholarships and student support at tribal colleges, including those in Michigan. The donation from philanthropist MacKenzie Scott will fund a seven-year plan to strengthen Native American higher education. Recent data pointed to longstanding […]
articles.content: Tribal colleges and universities operate more than 90 campuses and sites across 15 states, serving students from more than 250 federally recognized tribes, according to the Bureau of Indian Affairs. (Photo courtesy Saginaw Chippewa Tribal College)This story was originally published by Public News Service. A $70 million gift to the American Indian College Fund could help expand scholarships and student support at tribal colleges, including those in Michigan. The donation from philanthropist MacKenzie Scott will fund a seven-year plan to strengthen Native American higher education. Recent data pointed to longstanding funding shortages for tribal colleges. Carla Sineway, president of Saginaw Chippewa Tribal College in Mount Pleasant, said relying on temporary grants can make it difficult to maintain programs students depend on. “Many times when we get the funding, it’s very exciting, you get it for two or three years, and then the funding’s gone. And so, how do you sustain those programs? And so, you end up modifying,” Sineway explained. Sineway pointed out funding gaps can mean fewer staff and reduced student services. She noted the college also needs money for building maintenance and academic support. The American Indian College Fund says some of the donation will be used for coaching and career opportunities. The investment comes as Native American students continue to face barriers to higher education. According to U.S. Census figures, just 16% of American Indian and Alaska Native adults have earned a bachelor’s degree or higher, compared with 33% of adults nationally. Cheryl Crazy Bull, president and CEO of the American Indian College Fund, said increasing scholarship amounts is one way the organization hopes to make college more affordable. “We might have gone a few years ago from giving $500 a year in a scholarship to giving $1,500 a year – and now, our goal is to get to 3,000 a year,” Crazy Bull emphasized. She added an investment of $20 million in an endowment to support the organization’s long-term mission is also in the works.

SERVICE CIRCUIT: Veterans Day offers options to honor and help
articles.content: Veterans Day is Wednesday, Nov. 11 and the celebration of it is mixed with ceremonies and service projects. Saturday, Nov. 7, is the Royal Oak Veterans Committee’s annual Ruck 22 March to end veteran suicide. A ruck is a brisk military-style endurance walk while carrying weighted packs. Today’s participants ruck 2.2 miles carrying 22 pounds of food or personal items which then become donations. The main point of the ruck put on by the Royal Oak Veterans Events Committee is to raise awareness for veterans in crisis. Some studies show that about 22 of the nation’s veterans die by suicide each day. The ruck starts at 10 a.m. at the Royal Oak War Memorial located in the Barbara A. Hallman Memorial Plaza in Centennial Commons park at Troy Street and Second Street. It honors veterans and their families. “Vietnam Veterans of America Chapter 154 will be receiving a generous donation of food during Royal Oak Veterans Committee’s annual march to end veteran suicide,” Keith Edwards said. Edwards, a U.S. Air Force retiree, is the director of the food pantry run by the VVA chapter in Clinton Township. Volunteers will meet up at the Veterans of Foreign Wars Acorn Post 1669 in downtown Royal Oak. The VVA chapter’s trailer will be loaded up and then unloaded by the regular pantry crew. People may also donate food store gift cards. Any money donations collected at the ruck go to the John D. Dingell Veterans Affairs hospital in Detroit to support its programs dealing with the mental health of veterans. David Wandoff is the chair of the Royal Oak Veterans Events Committee that has done the ruck and the donation of food for about 10 years. “There is no registration for this event. We focus on military suicide awareness and donations to the VVA 154,” Wandoff said. “We have a group of volunteers that do this work which is always the Saturday before Veterans Day. Our ceremony is then. It’s the big part of our year. It’s kind of nice to be able to give back to the community this way. The ruck 22 is symbolic of the approximately 22 veterans that die by suicide every single day. It’s an informational campaign to show particularly veterans that we understand and that maybe we can help out a little bit by knowing and understanding what the veteran community is going through. “All the (money) donations go to the Veterans Crisis Line at the John Dingell VA to keep it going so that when people need to talk to somebody, they can just give a call and they have somebody they can talk to,” he said. The group sells hats with the number 22 on them and those proceeds go to the 24/7 crisis line which is: dial 988 then press 1; chat live or text 838255. See veteranscrisisline.net “It’s acknowledging and recognizing that there’s a problem and it’s something the veteran community fights disproportionately to the civilian population,” Wandoff said. “You join an organization, which is basically training you to push through pain and suffering and ignore all this stuff, and then emotionally, people have a hard time dealing with the repercussions of it. So, this is an effort to help people around veterans that might be suffering to be able to recognize and understand what they’re going through.” Centennial Commons park honors local people who have died in conflicts since the Civil War. The ruck venue will have informational booths as well. People unable to march may also donate money, or 22 items for veteran families, like hygiene products, baby items such as diapers, cold weather gear, first aid supplies, or bedding. There are several local Veterans Day observances. A ceremony at the Sterling Heights Community Center is at 11 a.m. Wednesday, Nov. 11 with keynote speaker Maj. Gen. Michelle Link. The VFW Lempke-Blackwell Post 7573 takes part in a ceremony at 11 a.m. Wednesday at the New Baltimore City Hall. The VVA chapter honor guard, The Point Team, participates in Resurrection Cemetery’s Veterans Day observance at 11 a.m. Wednesday at its outdoor American Veterans Memorial at 18201 Clinton River Road, Clinton Township. The Veterans Support Center where the food pantry is located is open from 9 to 11:30 a.m. — closing earlier than usual — so that chapter members can gather at the VFW Bruce Post 1146 in St. Clair Shores for a meeting and camaraderie. There is a Veterans Day breakfast 8-11:30 a.m. Wednesday at the War Memorial, Grosse Pointe. See warmemorial.org/events/veteransdaybreakfast2026 The event includes thank-you notes from students, a service song medley, and a gourmet breakfast. Medal of Honor recipient Terry Richardson is keynote speaker. Lions clubs get together on Nov. 14 to sponsor a bingo at the Michigan Veterans Home Chesterfield. According to MVH, about 45 years ago, 18 percent of U.S. adults were veterans. Today, about 6 percent of U.S. adults are veterans. Aspen Dental’s Day of Service is Saturday, Nov. 7. This is a day of free dental care for veterans, active military personnel, and family members. Call 844-277-3646 to see if openings are available at the Sterling Heights location. Riverview Family and Cosmetic Dentistry in St. Clair offers its 10th annual free dental services on Wednesday to veterans who are unemployed or low income who have no dental insurance. Call 810-328-5225. Numerous restaurants give free or discounted meals. See Military Wallet at tinyurl.com/58zuvrsx The Cathedral Church of St. Paul’s annual Veterans Day Service is at 4 p.m. Sunday, Nov. 8 at 4800 Woodward Avenue in midtown Detroit. Free lighted parking is available behind the cathedral, accessible from E. Warren Avenue via Cathedral Lane. “Our intent is to express profound appreciation for all who have dedicated themselves to protecting and serving others, while affirming our shared belief that war is never the answer and that peace may guide the future,” parish coordinator Erin McClellan said. “We will honor veterans and first responders, including those in state and local police and fire departments, whose daily service safeguards our communities.” Ask for details at info@detroitcathedral.org or call 313-833-4409. The service is live-streamed on the cathedral’s “our YouTube channel.” The Detroit Veterans Day Parade Corporation cancelled its annual events for this year due to construction on Michigan Avenue. The 2025 participants were invited to a ceremony and luncheon at the IBEW (Detroit Electrical Workers) Local 58 Detroit location. The parade is expected to return in 2027. This year is the 45th anniversary of the Vietnam Veterans Memorial in Washington, D.C. Beginning Nov. 7, the Vietnam Veterans Memorial Fund honors the more than 58,000 service members whose names are inscribed on The Wall through the daily virtual reading of the names. People may join online for the powerful tradition of remembrance, ensuring that each name is spoken aloud and each life is honored. See https://www.vvmf.org/45th Send news of service clubs and veterans organizations to Linda May at lindamay@ameritech.net or call landline 586-791-8116.
